title: A meme can be measured by which neurons fire
claim: The sources are Cammarata's essay 'Neural networks are already clean' (Goodfire, October 2026) and its technical companion, Tigges et al., 'Neurons as an Interpretable Basis' (Goodfire, 10 November 2026). The essay says most neurons in modern language models have one main job. The paper says most have one role or a few at strong activation. If so, a neuron is a ready-made unit, and a meme is whatever makes it fire.
verdict: Holds as a cheap, countable instrument. Not shown as the unit of culture. The essay's 90% is preliminary and self-graded. The companion paper's own figure is 69% of neuron poles with one job or one dominant job at strong activation, grouped by an LLM judge. Both are for models four times larger than the ones used here. The paper tests no cheap rival and no rewording, and the project has never steered or switched off a neuron. The field's survey of November 2026 still treats learned features, not neurons, as the default unit, while granting that superposition is unproven in large models and that MLP neurons are a privileged basis.

rungs.name: The reading is countable and repeatable
rungs.text: Batman has 1,534 neurons present in 23 or more of its 32 works. No random set of 32 films has one. Every unit has an address and can be read on any text. One caution from Goodfire's companion paper: it vouches only for the top and bottom 3% of a neuron's own activations. The study's presence rule is a rank among films and never checks that range.

rungs.name: Most neurons have one describable job
rungs.text: Goodfire's companion paper audits Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, not the 8B 4-bit models used here. In each pole's strongest 3% of firings, 47% of 5,468 poles have one job and 69% have one job or one dominant job, as grouped by an LLM judge. The essay said about 90% for Qwen3-32B. An outside retest of the essay got 57 to 78%, against 31% for random directions. One replication on small Qwen models found the labelling method called a randomly initialised network clean more often than the trained one.

rungs.name: The job is an idea, not a word
rungs.text: 24 of the 33 strongest Batman units were name or place detectors. Only 2 of 31 Qwen units were specific to their own rewording. Goodfire's companion paper, on a different model, runs no rewording test and no word-count rival. Several of its worked examples fire beside a set phrase. A few showcased units tell near-identical phrases apart, with no numbers. The essay says feeling neurons often fire on commas.

rungs.name: One meme lives in one neuron
rungs.text: The essay's examples need hubs of 4, 8 and 20 neurons for one concept. The companion paper agrees with the critics: concepts without their own neuron are carried by combinations of neurons. In its audit of Qwen3-32B, half the push toward the name Colorado takes 155 neurons and 80% takes 2,299. Design IN-24 tests one neuron against a few, a direction and a dictionary feature.

rungs.name: Neurons beat cheap rivals at measuring a text
rungs.text: On the primary model, word counts matched or beat neurons on every pre-registered test that had a word comparator: identity (0.80 against 0.52), heredity (11% against 16%), the residual test (p = 0.09 to 0.25). Random unselected neurons recovered sources better than the selected memes. Goodfire's companion paper compares neurons only with random directions and with chance, never with word counts, embeddings or an LLM reading the text.

rungs.name: Turning the neuron up writes the meme
rungs.text: Never tested here. Goodfire's companion paper steers one neuron and reports no numbers: raising a unit that fires on self-questioning made the model settle on an answer sooner. Elsewhere, single-neuron steering gives a clean, consistent effect for a small minority of neurons (130 of 294,912 in one 2026 census of a small Qwen), and the neuron that reads a concept is often not the one that writes it. The 2026 survey makes this the test of a label: a unit stands for a concept only if changing it shifts the output, measured against random units of matched size.

rungs.name: Neurons list every meme a model knows
rungs.text: Rejected by all sides, Cammarata and the companion paper included: 'we do not see a perfect one-to-one mapping of meaning to neurons'. Models are thought to hold more facts and features than they have neurons, though the 2026 survey calls that a hypothesis for large models. A new meme the model never learned has no neuron at all.

title: The measurement carries over between models
claim: The hope is that different models converge on the same neurons, so a meme measured in one can be mapped to another. The paper cites three results for this: universal neurons in GPT-2, the platonic representation hypothesis, and unpaired translation between embedding spaces.
verdict: True for coarse geometry, partly true for directions with a learned map, mostly false for individual neurons. The three cited papers support only the weakest reading, and the first is evidence against. P1 and P2 also pull against each other: the units that match best across models are the ones a single word reproduces. The field's survey of November 2026 draws the same line: shared algorithms are the supported kind of convergence, shared representations the less supported kind.

rungs.name: Two models agree on which texts are alike
rungs.text: Qwen and Llama distance matrices correlate at 0.98. But random neurons give 0.90 to 0.93 and two word methods agree at 0.92. Real, cheap, and mostly a fact about the texts. In the literature, local neighbourhoods agree; one shared global geometry is contested by two 2026 papers. The 2026 survey calls evidence of this kind fragile.

rungs.name: A direction can be mapped with paired text
rungs.text: In one unreviewed study of 7B models, about half of matched feature pairs pass a correlation of 0.6. A joint dictionary has already been trained on this project's exact pair, Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B. Paired text is free here. The project has not tried any learned map. The 2026 survey warns that joint dictionaries can report a feature as unique to one model when both have it.

rungs.name: The same individual neurons recur
rungs.text: Gurnee et al. found 1 to 5% of GPT-2 neurons universal across retrainings of the same architecture, and concluded neurons are not the right unit. Here, the median twin across all 14,843 families is r = 0.40 against 0.36 for random units. A 2026 study of models up to 30B parameters finds that neurons shared between independently trained models are a shrinking share as models grow. Goodfire's companion paper studies one model and maps nothing between models.

rungs.name: Agreement goes beyond shared words
rungs.text: The 0.82 twins are matched by equally word-like control units (0.86). With names removed the same pairs fall to 0.14. Concept units keep an edge on original text only (0.62 against 0.46). The two models' revenge units correlate at 0.39.

rungs.name: It holds across languages
rungs.text: Not tested here. Elsewhere, middle-layer features inside one model fire for a concept whatever the language, which is the best evidence that word-free units exist at all. Designs UN-22 and LI-22 test it.

rungs.name: It holds across media
rungs.text: The poster experiment is not a test: one image per work, no rival, and no link between text units and image units.

rungs.name: It carries to human readers
rungs.text: No human has validated anything in the project: labels, judges, reviewers and fact-checker were all AI. Model-to-brain fits exist but are coarse, and most of the fit is reproduced by word rate and position.
